A soffit is the underside — the bottom-facing surface — of a structural part of a building that hangs overhead. Think of it this way: whenever something architectural is above you and you look up at its underside, that surface you're looking at is a soffit.

The word always refers to a surface that faces downward from something built above.
The Most Common Soffit: The Roof Overhang

The place most people encounter a soffit is on the outside of a house, under the edge of the roof.

Most roofs extend slightly beyond the walls of a building — this jutting-out section is called the eave or overhang. Now, if you stand close to the wall of a house and tilt your head back to look upward at the roof's edge, the flat surface you see above you — the one "tucked in" between the outer wall and the roof's edge — that horizontal panel is the soffit.

It's essentially the ceiling of the roof's overhang.

Here's a simple way to picture it:

  • Imagine a shelf sticking out from a wall.
  • The top of the shelf is the roof.
  • The sides are the fascia boards (the vertical boards you see at the roof's edge).
  • The underside of that shelf — the part you'd see if you crouched and looked up — is the soffit.
Soffits in Other Parts of a Building

The term isn't limited to roofs. The same word is used for the underside of many architectural elements:

Staircases: When you look at a staircase from the side or from underneath, there's a slanted surface angling downward from the top step to the floor. That sloped underside is a soffit. It's the reason the space under a staircase exists — soffits sometimes hide the structural "guts" underneath.

Arches: When you walk through a stone or brick archway, the curved surface that forms the underside of the arch — the part that faces straight down at you — is the soffit of the arch (sometimes also called the intrados, but soffit is the broader architectural term used for this surface).

Beams and lintels: A beam is a horizontal structural bar stretching across a space. Its bottom face — the surface facing the floor — is its soffit.

Balconies: If you're standing on the ground below a balcony and look up, the flat underside of the balcony's floor slab or deck is a soffit.

Kitchen cabinets: Many older kitchens have a boxed-in structure built above the upper cabinets to fill the gap between the cabinet tops and the ceiling. The underside of that box — looking down at you while you cook — is a soffit.

Since soffits are essentially protective and finishing surfaces, they're built from materials chosen for durability and looks:

  • Vinyl — the most common in modern homes; lightweight, cheap, and resistant to moisture.
  • Aluminum — durable and weather-resistant, used in both residential and commercial buildings.
  • Wood — traditional and attractive, but requires regular painting or sealing to prevent rot.
  • Fiber cement — a tougher, longer-lasting option that mimics the look of wood.

Soffits aren't just decorative finishing touches. They serve real, practical purposes:

1. Protection: Without a soffit, the underside of your roof's overhang would expose raw rafters (the wooden structural beams) directly to rain, moisture, insects, and birds. A soffit seals all of that up and protects the structure.

2. Pest prevention: An open eave is an open invitation for birds, squirrels, wasps, and bats to nest inside your roof's structure. A solid soffit keeps them out.

3. Ventilation: This is a clever and important one. Many soffits — especially on homes — are vented soffits, meaning they have small perforated holes or slots built into them. These allow cool outside air to flow in from the eave level, travel up through the attic, and exit through vents at the top of the roof (called ridge vents). This steady airflow prevents the attic from overheating in summer and prevents moisture buildup in winter that would otherwise cause mold or structural damage.

4. Finished appearance: Perhaps most obviously, a soffit gives an otherwise rough or unfinished underside of a structure a clean, polished look. Without it, buildings would show their structural "skeleton" in unattractive ways.

If you're ever unsure whether something is a soffit, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is it part of a building structure (not furniture or separate objects)?
  2. Is it the underside — the bottom-facing surface — of that structure?

If both answers are yes, it's a soffit.

A soffit is the finished underside of any architectural structure that projects or extends overhead — most commonly the underside of a roof overhang, but also found under arches, stairs, beams, balconies, and built-in cabinets. It serves to protect structural elements, block pests, allow ventilation, and give a building a tidy, finished appearance. Whenever you look upward at the underside of something built overhead — that surface is a soffit.
